about: The plan for the lines of docs/woodex-os/14-PRODUCTION-TODO.md that are not done: a short title for each, the rounds in which the lines that can start now are done, and for each of those lines what is built and how it is tested. Read with the list by scripts/verify-plan.mjs, which writes docs/woodex-os/21-PENDING-WORK-PLAN-AND-TESTS.md and fails when the three disagree. When a line is done, take it out of its round and out of the titles.

rounds.name: The addresses the owner listed: series, filters and search
rounds.why: The owner's list of 27 November names three addresses of `/api/v1` that do not exist yet. They are what a shop needs when it stops reading the whole catalogue: a list of the series, what a list can be narrowed by, and a search. First of the freed lines, because the next (the cost of an open page) is easier once the shop no longer has to hold everything.

lines.found: The contract of `/api/v1` has ten addresses, seven of them read. The series come inside the answer of `/catalogue/categories`. The list of products is narrowed by `category`, `series` and `since`, in pages of at most 100. Nothing answers at `/catalogue/series`, `/catalogue/filters` or `/catalogue/search`: the last route of the group says 404. The shop reads the whole catalogue page after page and narrows and searches it in the browser (`apps/storefront/src/pages/Shop.tsx`: the search box compares the words typed with the names it has read).
build: `GET /api/v1/catalogue/series`: the published series, each with its address, its name and how many published products it holds.

`GET /api/v1/catalogue/filters`: what the list can be narrowed by, counted over the published products only: the categories and the series with their counts, the lowest and the highest price of what has one, and how many are priced on request.
`GET /api/v1/catalogue/search`: the words typed, at least two signs, compared with the name and the code of each published product; a page of products in the shape of the list.
The three are written into the contract first, are answered through `ApiAnswer`, and are counted with the other reads, by the visitor.
The shop's server hands them on, and the shop's list takes its filters and its counts from the answer instead of working them out.
tests: The contract test: the three addresses key by key, for every status the contract documents.

The admin's suite: a draft, a withdrawn and an archived product is in no count, no filter and no search result; a search finds a product by a word of its name and by its code, whatever the capitals; one sign is refused by the code the contract names.
The shop's reader script: the filters and counts shown are the ones the admin answered.
browser: The product journey gains a step: the visitor finds the published product by typing its code into the shop's search, and no longer finds it after the publication is withdrawn.
lines.against: With a draft counted in a filter, the test of the counts names it; with the search reading the saved draft, the test names the draft's name.
lines.back: The shop's switch stays off, so no visitor sees any of it. The three addresses hand out nothing the list does not hand out already.

rounds.name: One code, one product: held by the database
rounds.why: The rule of 27 November (DL-049) is checked by reading the other products, which two editors can pass in the same moment. It follows the addresses because the search of that round finds a product by its code, and a code that names two products would answer with both.

lines.found: A code another product has is refused when a draft is saved and again at publication (`ProductCatalogue::refuseACodeOfAnotherProduct`): the check reads the saved and the published copies of every other product, archived or not. A code is a value inside the saved draft, not a column, so no index holds it. Two editors who give two products the same new code in the same moment can both pass the check when they save; the second publication is then refused, and until then two drafts carry one code.
build: A table of codes: one row for each code that a product's saved draft or published copy carries, in one spelling, with a unique index.

Saving a draft and publishing write the product's rows in the same transaction as the product. A code that another product holds fails on the index, and the editor is told as today, on the row of the code.
A migration fills the table from the products there are. Where two products already share a code it stops, lists them, and changes nothing.
tests: The admin's suite: the rules of DL-049 as they stand, each asked of the table: a code taken, a code freed by a changed draft, a code kept by the published copy, the same code in other capitals.
The two-writers command gains a step: two saves of the same new code in the same moment, fifty runs, on MySQL 8.4, MariaDB 10.11 and MariaDB 11.4: one is refused every time.
The migration on a copy of the 170 imported products: every code is in the table once.
browser: The product journey, unchanged, on the new table: its code is typed once and accepted.
lines.against: With the unique index left out, the two-writers step reports two products with one code.
lines.back: The migration's way back drops the table; the check that reads the other products is still there.

rounds.name: What an open page of the shop costs the admin's host
rounds.why: Measured in the round of 28 November. It does not stand in the way of the switch for a few visitors, and it does for many: the host is shared hosting, and every read of every open page is a request it has to answer.

lines.found: Measured on the rehearsal with the link on: a page of the shop that stands open and is not touched asks the admin nine times a minute through the shop's server: the categories and the replaced photographs every fifteen seconds, the whole list of products once a minute. A journey of ten pages asked 34 times in under a minute. The list takes `since` and the shop does not send it. The admin allows one visitor 120 reads a minute (D-082), which fourteen open pages of one visitor reach; the shop's server then answers 503 for the catalogue.
build: The shop's server keeps what it read of the admin for a few seconds and answers every visitor from it: one read at the admin for all the pages that ask in that time. It keeps only what is public and the same for everybody: the categories, the products, the list of replaced photographs. An answer that is an error is not kept, and a basket is never answered from what is kept.
An open page asks whether anything changed since its last reading, and reads the list again only then.
How long a withdrawn product may still be shown is one number of the shop's server, written down: fifteen seconds at most.
tests: The bridges' script: many requests within the time are one read at the admin; after the time, a new read; an error is not kept; nothing a visitor writes is kept.
The reader's script: with nothing changed since the last reading, the page reads nothing more.
A measurement kept with the report: fifty pages opened on the rehearsal, and the reads the admin received in a minute.
browser: The product journey: after "Withdraw", the product is gone from the shop within fifteen seconds, and the journey says how long it took.
lines.against: With the time set to an hour, the journey's step 17 fails: the withdrawn product is still shown.
lines.back: The time is a setting of the shop's server; 0 asks the admin every time, as today.

rounds.name: The code style and the analyser in CI
rounds.why: Two checks exist and no workflow runs them (the audit of 23 November, AU-16). Small, and it protects every round after it.

lines.found: No workflow runs the code style (`composer lint`) or the analyser (`composer analyse`): the audit of 23 November, AU-16. Run in the sandbox on the code of 28 November (PHP 8.5): the style check names 16 files of 1,264, fifteen of them tests; the analyser reports 147 errors in 36 files of `app/` at level 6. None is in a file of the last two rounds. The comparison of the live shop's database with its schema files says "Production is unverified this run" on every run: no read-only address is given to it.
build: `os-ci.yml` runs `composer lint` and `composer analyse` on every push that touches `platform/`; a pull request fails on either.

What the two report on the day is cured in the same round: the 16 files are rewritten by the tool, and each of the 147 errors is cured in the code or, where the analyser is wrong, named in a list with its reason. The first run is then green, and a later fault is somebody's own.

The comparison of the live shop's database with its schema files runs when a read-only address is given as a secret; without one the run carries an error that names what is missing, instead of a notice nobody reads. The address is the owner's to give.
tests: On the round's own branch: a file of `app/` with a style fault fails the run and the run names the file; taken out, the run passes. The same with a type fault for the analyser.
lines.against: The two faults above are the test: each is pushed once and taken out again.
lines.back: The two steps are taken out of the workflow.

rounds.name: Two small cures of the live shop
rounds.why: Both are findings of the audit of 23 November (AU-11, AU-23) that need nobody and change what a visitor and a search engine are told.

lines.found: The last rule of the shop's `vercel.json` hands every address that is no file to the shop's page (`/:path*` to `/index.html`) with the status 200. The page then says "not found" and asks not to be indexed (since 25 November); the status is still success. Read on 23 November: `/this-page-is-not-there` answered 200. The shop's own server answers 404 for the same address.
build: The addresses the shop has are written down once, where the build already knows them for its static pages and its sitemap: the fixed pages, and the patterns of a product, a category, a series, an article and a published page.
On Vercel an address that fits none of them is answered by the shop's server, which already answers `/api` and the sitemap there: the not-found page, with the status 404.
tests: A script reads `vercel.json` against the shop's routes: every route of the application is named, and an address that fits none goes to the server.
The check of the live sites asks for an address that is not there and requires 404.
browser: The crawl of the built shop: every address of the sitemap answers 200; five addresses that are not there answer 404 and show the not-found page.
lines.against: With the last rule put back, the new point of the live check fails.
lines.back: The one rule put back in `vercel.json`.

lines.found: The shop asks Google for the font Inter on every page, twice: a link in `apps/storefront/index.html` (six weights) and an `@import` in `apps/storefront/src/index.css` (seven). The admin carries its font as files of its own build. Every run of the browser scripts in the sandbox, which reaches no other server, reports the file that did not arrive.
build: Inter as files of the shop's build, with its licence, declared in the stylesheet with `font-display: swap`.
Both references to Google are taken out.
tests: The build's own check refuses `fonts.googleapis.com` and `fonts.gstatic.com` anywhere in the built shop.
browser: The crawl: no request leaves for another server, and a heading and a paragraph are set in Inter at both widths.
lines.against: With the link put back in `index.html`, the build's check fails.

rounds.name: The timer, still to be read from the live site
rounds.why: One small line whose building is merged and whose proof can only come from the live site: GitHub starts a timer when it will. Nothing is built here; the line is closed by reading, and the readings are written down at the start of every round. The two lines that stood here with it are done: the long life of the built files (T-152) was read on 20 November, and the third cold start (T-154) on 21 November.

lines.found: The timer was written again with pull request #52: 03:47, 09:47, 15:47 and 21:47 UTC, from 20 November at 15:02 UTC. Before that, six timed runs came for thirteen times due: the times due at 06:23 and 18:23 UTC brought a run every time, 1 h 08 min to 2 h 43 min late, and the times due at 00:23 and 12:23 UTC never. Read on 21 November at 12:26 UTC: two runs for four times due at the new minute. 15:47 UTC on 20 November brought none; 21:47 UTC brought a run at 22:22 UTC, green; 03:47 UTC on 21 November brought none; 09:47 UTC brought a run at 11:49 UTC, 2 h 02 min late. That run failed, and rightly: it is the first timed run that found a live site changed (issue #54, cured with pull request #55). The change had stood for four hours by then. Eight timed runs in all, five of them green; the two of 18 and 19 November failed on a point of the check itself (issue #46, cured with pull request #47). Starting the check by hand is refused to this session (HTTP 403). The check after a merge has run every time.
build: Nothing more is built. GitHub's list of timed runs is read at the start of every round, and how many of the times due brought a run is written into the list.

If the new minute does no better after eight times due, the line says that GitHub does not keep a six-hourly timer for this repository, and the owner is asked whether twice a day is enough or another service should start the check.
tests: Runs started by the timer are in GitHub's list for at least three of the last four times due at the new minute, and they are green.
lines.against: Done on 17 November: a forced failure opened issue #38, and the next proof closed it.

rounds.name: Without a mouse; help, pinned and recent screens
rounds.why: T-054 is P1, and the accessibility review of gate A waits for it. The new entries of the top bar get their keyboard tests from the first day.

lines.found: The search opens with Ctrl+K and answers to the arrow keys and Escape. The journeys press Ctrl+K once and Escape three times. No task is done by keyboard alone: the sidebar, the focus inside a dialog and the announcing of a refused field are untested.
build: A third journey, done by keyboard only: sign in; the sidebar, a group opened and a link followed; the search opened, a screen found, chosen, and Escape giving the focus back; a dialog and a drawer that keep the focus inside and return it; a lead and a quotation made; a refused field announced where it stands.
What the journey finds is corrected in the same round.
tests: The journey runs with the other two, in the sandbox and in CI.
A test reads every dialog for its name, and every field with an error for the link to its message.
lines.against: With the dialog no longer keeping the focus inside, the journey fails at that step.
lines.back: Tests, and small corrections to views.
lines.yours: After it, one person of your team does the same without a mouse, and with a screen reader if one is at hand. Gate A asks for that review.

lines.found: The top bar has the search, "Create new", the colour theme, the notifications and the account. It has no help entry, and no pinned or recent screens. A person's record has no place for such preferences yet.
build: A Help entry in the top bar: what this screen is for, the keyboard shortcuts, and the request number to give when asking for help.
A screen can be pinned from its heading; pinned screens stand at the head of the menu. The screens opened last are listed, for each person.
Both are kept with the person, in one small table added by a migration.
tests: Pinned and recent screens are remembered for each person and are still there after signing out and in.
Nobody is shown another person's; a screen the person may no longer open is not offered.
All of it by keyboard, in the journey of T-054.
browser: The crawl at both widths; the keyboard journey pins a screen and opens it from the menu.
lines.against: With the check of the person's rights taken out, "is not offered" fails.
lines.back: One migration that only adds; its way back removes the table.

rounds.name: Every shared part on one screen; a slow list and a lost connection
rounds.why: Both waited for the shared table (T-041), and both are P2. The first is a criterion of gate A ("shared component examples"). The second finishes the five states: the table can say "loading" since 20 November and no screen says it.

lines.found: No screen shows the shared parts side by side. The parts are 25 files in `platform/resources/views/components/admin` and the three parts of the table beside them; their rules are written there since 20 November (`README.md`). A new screen is a 69th destination: the registry of destinations, Feature status and the tests that count destinations change with it.
build: One screen under System, for owner and admin: every shared part in each of its states, drawn by the part itself with sample values, never by a copy of its markup. Buttons, badges, cards, fields with and without an error, the empty state, the dialog, the toast, the page links, and the table in its five states.
The destination is added to the registry with its permission, so that the menu, Feature status and the route agree.
tests: The screen opens for owner and admin and is refused to the other roles.
A test lists the files under `components/admin`: a part that is not drawn on the screen, and is not on a short written list of parts that cannot stand alone, fails it.
The table's five states on the screen are read with the words and roles the component's own test reads.
browser: The crawl opens it at 1366 px and 390 px: no console error, nothing wider than the window. It is looked at in the dark theme, and one picture of it goes into the report for gate A.
lines.against: With one part taken off the screen, the test that lists the parts names it.
lines.back: A screen that changes no record. It can be taken out of the registry alone.

lines.found: No screen says "loading": a Livewire screen arrives with its rows, and no component is loaded late. `wire:loading` is written 117 times in 64 views, to dim rows or to stop a button being pressed twice. Nothing tells a person that the connection is lost: `wire:offline` is written nowhere and no script listens for it, so a press then does nothing and says nothing. The shared table has had a loading state since 20 November (T-041).
build: A notice in the top bar while the browser is offline or the server does not answer, and that it is back when it is: said to a screen reader, and never laid over the form a person is typing in.
A press that could not be sent says so, and what was typed stays.

With the network slowed on the rehearsal, each list of the shared table is timed. A list that is slow there is loaded late and draws the table's loading state first; a list that arrives in time is left as it is, and the report names both kinds.
tests: A test draws the notice and reads its words and its role.
For each list that is loaded late: what stands there first is the table's loading state, and the rows that follow are the rows of before.
browser: A journey step cuts the network with the browser's own switch, presses Save on a form, reads the notice, brings the network back and saves: nothing typed is lost.
With the network slowed, the placeholder of a late list is seen and then replaced by its rows.
lines.against: With the notice taken out, the journey step fails where it reads it.
lines.back: Views and one small script; the built files change. The notice can be taken out alone, and a late list made an early one again by one word.

rounds.name: Lighter pages; nothing smaller than 12 px
rounds.why: Both change the same shared parts: the menu, the top bar, the search.

lines.found: By the crawl's figures in the list (§17): a near-empty page is 144 KB of HTML, 15.6 KB compressed. About 110 KB of it is the menu, the search's templates and the icons, sent again with every page. The median page is 161 KB.
build: First a measurement, part by part.

Then, as far as the measurement says: each icon drawn once and referred to; the search's list of screens fetched when the search is first opened; the phone's menu made of the same markup as the sidebar.
tests: A test holds a near-empty page under 60 KB of HTML and prints the size of each part.
The crawl prints the median size of all pages.
The journeys that use the search, the menu and the phone's drawer pass.
browser: Both journeys and the crawl at both widths.
lines.against: The size test fails on today's page.

lines.found: 19 places in 14 views, and 7 rules of the stylesheets, set text below 12 px: from 8 px (the line under the logo) to 11 px.
build: Each is raised to 12 px. Where a label then no longer fits, the layout gives way, not the size.
tests: A test reads every view and every rule of the stylesheets: none sets text below 12 px.
The crawl measures the text as it is drawn on every page at both widths and fails below 12 px.
lines.against: One 10 px label put back fails both.
lines.back: Views and the stylesheets; the bundle is rebuilt and committed.
lines.yours: If a place cannot take 12 px, it is shown to you as a named exception to accept or refuse.

rounds.name: The content policy without `eval`
rounds.why: After the rounds that replace whole parts of the views (the table, the dashboard, the top bar, the menu), so that nothing is converted twice; and before the screen pass, which its test then holds to the strict form from the first view.

lines.found: About 200 Alpine expressions in the views: 21 `x-data`, 19 of them written out in the markup; 121 handlers of events; 30 `x-show`.
build: Livewire's build for a strict policy is switched on, and every expression in the views is read against what it accepts.
The longer ones become named components in the admin's own script; the bundle is rebuilt and committed.
`'unsafe-eval'` leaves the policy.
tests: The policy test pins the header word for word, without `'unsafe-eval'`.
A test reads every view and refuses an expression the strict build cannot read.
Both journeys and the crawl of every screen with the policy enforced: nothing refused.
The outside check requires the header without `'unsafe-eval'` after the merge.
browser: Both journeys, and every screen as four roles at both widths. The scripts already fail on anything the browser refuses.
lines.against: With one arrow function left in a view, the crawl reports the refusal and fails.
lines.back: `SECURITY_CSP=report` or `off` on the site; or the strict build off and the word back in the policy, in one commit.

rounds.name: The screen pass, area by area
rounds.why: P1, and last all the same: it is the largest line, several rounds of its own, one for each area in the order you set (DL-008): E-commerce, CRM, Sales, then the others. Every round before it changes a part it builds on.

lines.found: 3,109 uses of a grey written directly, in 145 views: the most in Sales, CRM and System. 1,807 dark-theme variants are written by hand. Colours written as numbers are mostly in the PDF and mail templates, which must carry their own; those stay as they are.
build: In each area: greys move to the theme's roles; what is selected takes the theme's green; each page follows the patterns of document 05 §8; its lists use the table of T-041, and are drawn as cards on a phone (T-042) where people work the list from a phone.
The dark theme is looked at on every screen of the area.
